sm: Host Jag of the Atlas Society welcomes author Noah Rothman to discuss his book Blood and Progress: A Century of Leftwing Violence. Rothman explains that he started as a theater kid, but after the September 11th attacks moved into news talk radio, then studied security policy in the former Soviet space and became a writer in 2010. The book grew out of a Commentary magazine essay commissioned in December 2024 after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. Rothman describes the celebration of the killing by entertainers and the "but" that Democratic politicians attached to their condemnations, which he says implies a call for total societal upheaval.

Rothman says the issue is never the issue; it is always the revolution, an insight he credits to David Horowitz. He recounts watching his parents' fear during the 1991 Soviet coup as a nine-year-old, and says the things he studies are the things that scare him, including nuclear weapons, communism and revolutionary street violence. Asked about the Democratic midterm wins, he says the big, varied majorities may let leadership sideline the radical left. But he warns that the same outcome could radicalize those on the far left who feel the system ignores their demands, leading them either to withdraw or to attack the system. The host then raises a podcast clip joking about digging up Charlie Kirk.

Asked why the falsehood persists that Kirk's accused killer, Tyler Robinson, was a MAGA person, Rothman says it gives callous figures permission to feel they are still on the good side. He says the claims began within hours of the September 2025 assassination, and notes that CBS floated a "nihilistic violent extremism" theory, a category he says the FBI does not use. He says a YouGov poll found a plurality believed a right-winger did it. On the statistic that 76 percent of extremist murders are from the right, he traces it to the Anti-Defamation League, and criticizes the University of Cincinnati's database for counting things like graffiti, a homeless man's racial slurs, and gang or family violence as right-wing violence.

Rothman says these database builders do not want real answers, and he cites a 2021 Department of Homeland Security document describing how researchers of left-wing extremism face smear campaigns, isolation and threats. He says political violence is reciprocal, with each side convinced the state favors the other. Answering a viewer question, he says the book covers three waves of left-wing violence: the anarchist and labor violence of the 1910s, the Marxist guerrilla groups of the 1960s through early 1980s, and today's. He cites the Haymarket bombing, the Palmer raids, Luigi Galleani, Emma Goldman and the 1910 Los Angeles Times bombing. Each earlier wave ended when policing and the movements' own attacks on innocents turned the public against them, which he says has not yet happened in the third wave.

Asked whether revolutionary ideologies are inherently violent, Rothman says socialist and collectivist revolutions are especially tied to violence, unlike America's largely conservative revolution. He traces the Bolsheviks' admiration for the Jacobins and quotes Robespierre's line that terror is an emanation of virtue. He says the terror in France became class-based, and Lenin abandoned individual guilt in favor of categories of people, quoting the Chekist Martin Latsis that what matters is what class a person belongs to. Rothman says today's tendency to treat people as members of categories, whether to punish or to elevate them, similarly paves the way for violence.

Rothman continues that flattening individuals into categories dehumanizes them and gives license for violence. Asked about Europe, he says the 1960s and 70s American groups, such as the Weather Underground, Black Liberation Army and FALN, were Cuba-oriented and favored foco-style small-cell violence. He recommends Jason Burke's book The Revolutionists, which shows similar groups abroad drifting from Marxism to pan-Arabism to Islamism, suggesting violence, not ideology, was the constant. He says today's left looks more like that European pattern. He then describes the Soviet Union's campaign of "Zionology" after losing the 1967 and 1973 wars, demonizing Israel with racist and Nazi comparisons, a legacy he says still lingers.

Rothman says the KGB forged racist letters attributed to the Jewish Defense League and backed the UN's Zionism-is-racism resolution, and that the campaign's legacy outlived the Soviets. Asked about common rhetorical moves, he lists propaganda of the deed, small leaderless cells, attacks on law enforcement, and the idea that systemic oppression licenses violence. He describes a 2025 attack by a ten-member left-wing cell on a Texas Border Patrol office, with literature and banners advocating proletarian revolution, which wounded two officers. He also describes a gunman angry about football-related brain injury who entered a Manhattan high-rise and killed real estate executive Wesley LeBlanc, after which some online commenters celebrated the killing.

Rothman says Maya Sulkin documented the online audience that cheered that killing as revolutionary vengeance, and that some people see a path to power in nursing such violent delusions. Asked about Assata Shakur, he describes her as a Black Liberation Army member convicted in the 1973 New Jersey killing of trooper Werner Foerster, broken out of prison in 1979 and living in Cuba until she died last September. He says she has been celebrated by campuses, media and NPR, which he calls a morally empty effort to give left-wing violence virtue. On young people, he cites surveys: about one in five in 2017, 41 percent at Yale in 2022, and FIRE's 2025 finding that 34 percent found violence to stop speech acceptable, with only 58 percent of Gen Z rejecting it.

Rothman says the FIRE data suggests the acceptance of political violence is no longer contained to campuses and spreads through social media and workplaces. On whether social media causes radicalization, he says it is both an amplifier and a tool for hostile foreign actors, but the real problem is demand for radical extremism. He says he has no pat answer, but offers about half a dozen recommendations, such as dispelling the idea that terrorism stems from poverty and shrinking politics back to elections and legislation rather than everything in life. He calls for a more responsible political class, noting that high office now attracts the radical, the narcissistic or the wealthy. Jag praises the book, mentions the Atlas Society's educational work, and previews next week's guest, Joel Trammell.
